name: How Models Are Trained
intent: Follow a language model from a blank network to a helpful assistant: learning to predict text, then to follow instructions, then to prefer the answers people choose.
scenario: A team tries a freshly pretrained model. Asked 'What is the capital of France?', it writes five more quiz questions instead of answering. Another stage of training is needed before it behaves like an assistant.
problem: Nothing in a network says what language is, or what a good answer is. All of that has to come from data and from a measure of how wrong the network currently is. Each training stage uses a different kind of data and a different measure, and each changes the model in a different way. Knowing which stage does what explains why a model can write fluent text and still ignore an instruction, or make up a fact.

howItWorks.title: Pretraining: predict the next token
howItWorks.text: The model reads very large amounts of text and, at every position, guesses the next token. The loss is the cross-entropy: how little probability the model gave to the token that actually came next. Nobody labels this data, because the text itself contains the answers.

howItWorks.title: Gradient descent nudges every weight
howItWorks.text: Backpropagation works out how the loss would change if each weight changed a little. Every weight is then moved a small step in the direction that lowers the loss. The step size is set by the learning rate, and in practice an optimizer such as Adam adjusts it for each weight. This repeats over many batches of text.

howItWorks.title: Supervised fine-tuning: learn to follow instructions
howItWorks.text: The pretrained model is trained further on examples of a request and a good response, written or chosen by people. The same loss is used, but the data now shows the behaviour wanted: answer the question, keep to the format.

howItWorks.title: Preference tuning: learn which answer people choose
howItWorks.text: People compare answers and say which is better. In RLHF, as in the InstructGPT paper, a reward model is trained on those comparisons and the language model is then improved against it with reinforcement learning. Direct preference optimization (DPO) skips the separate reward model and the reinforcement learning loop, and trains on the preference pairs directly.

howItWorks.title: What each stage changes
howItWorks.text: Pretraining gives the model its knowledge and language ability. Instruction tuning and preference tuning mainly shape how it behaves: following requests, tone, refusing some things. In the InstructGPT study, raters preferred the answers of a tuned 1.3-billion-parameter model to those of the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3.

howItWorks.title: What training cannot add
howItWorks.text: A model knows what was in its data up to a cutoff date. Later stages of training make it more helpful, but they do not give it today's news, and a tuned model can still follow instructions badly or state things that are not true.

pros: Pretraining needs no labels, so it can use enormous amounts of ordinary text
Pretraining and supervised fine-tuning use the same next-token loss, so one training stack covers most of the work
A few thousand good examples can change behaviour a lot at the fine-tuning stage
Preference data captures things that are hard to write as rules, such as tone and helpfulness
cons: Pretraining is very expensive and cannot be repeated casually
The model is only as good, and as fair, as the text and the preferences it was trained on
Preference tuning can teach a model to please raters rather than to be right
The knowledge stops at the data cutoff, and later training does not fix that
whenToUse: You need to explain why a base model and an assistant model behave so differently
You are deciding whether a problem calls for prompting, retrieval or more training
You are reading a model card and need to know what the training stages mean
whenNotToUse: Do not expect fine-tuning to teach reliable new facts: retrieval is usually a better way to add knowledge
Do not use preference tuning to fix a data problem that supervised examples would solve more simply
Do not draw conclusions about a named commercial model's training from the published studies of others
pitfalls: Setting the learning rate too high, so the loss rises instead of falling
Training on the evaluation data by accident, so the scores look better than the model is
Treating a model's confident tone as a sign that the facts are right
Fine-tuning on a small, narrow set until the model forgets how to do other things

roles.label: Training data
roles.description: Raw text for pretraining, then examples of requests and answers, then comparisons between answers.

roles.label: Model weights
roles.description: The numbers that are adjusted. They hold what the model has learned.

roles.label: Loss
roles.description: A single number for how wrong the model currently is on the data it just saw.

roles.label: Gradient step
roles.description: Moves each weight a little in the direction that lowers the loss.

quiz.question: A freshly pretrained model answers 'What is the capital of France?' by writing more quiz questions. What is the best explanation?
options: The model has not stored any facts about France, so it fills the space with other text
Pretraining only taught it to continue text, so instruction tuning is needed to teach it to answer requests
The learning rate was too low, so the model never learned to stop writing after a question
The model is too small, and a larger model would always answer questions straight away
quiz.explanation: Predicting the next token teaches the model to continue text in the style it has seen, and a list of quiz questions is a likely continuation. Supervised fine-tuning on request and answer pairs, and then preference tuning, teach it to respond to a request. Size and learning rate are not the cause.

quiz.question: A model's training data stops in 2023. Users ask about last week's events and it makes up answers. A colleague proposes fine-tuning it on thousands of instruction examples. Will that fix the problem?
options: Yes, because instruction examples teach the model every fact it needs for new questions
Yes, but only if the examples are written in the same format as the users' questions
No, because fine-tuning always removes the knowledge the model had after pretraining
No, because tuning mainly changes behaviour, and fresh facts are better supplied by retrieval at question time
quiz.explanation: Instruction tuning changes how the model responds, and it is a poor and costly way to add facts that keep changing. Supplying current documents at question time, as retrieval does, handles fresh information. Fine-tuning does not always erase knowledge, and a matching format does not add facts.

quiz.question: In a toy training run, the loss falls steadily, then the learning rate is raised sharply and the loss shoots up to huge numbers. What does this most likely show?
options: The steps overshoot the minimum by more each time, so training diverges and the rate must be lowered
The model has finished learning, and the larger loss is a sign that it is ready to be used
The data was too clean, so the larger learning rate adds the noise that the model needs
The loss function is wrong, and a different one would always give a falling curve
quiz.explanation: With a step that is too big, each update jumps past the minimum and lands further away, so the loss grows. Lowering the learning rate restores a falling loss. A rising loss is not a sign of finished learning, and the cause is the step size, not the data or the loss function.
